overview.title: 📖 Overview: Finishing Standing and Valuation, and the Burial List
overview.subtitle: Temurah 33a–33b
overview.hebrewSource: וְהֶעֱמִיד אֶת הַבְּהֵמָה לִפְנֵי הַכֹּהֵן, וְהֶעֱרִיךְ הַכֹּהֵן אֹתָהּ בֵּין טוֹב וּבֵין רָע
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf finishes the Rabbi Yoḥanan–Reish Lakish dispute by mining a single phrase. Rav shows how 'whether it be good or bad' supports Reish Lakish, and how the restrictive word 'it' (אֹתָהּ) must exclude something from standing and valuation — the two amoraim differ over what. Two baraitot are then thrown at each position, and each amora answers by fixing which kind of blemish the baraita means, with Reish Lakish going so far as to reverse a text. A new mishna then opens with two lists: sacred items that must be buried, and forbidden items that must be burned.

slides.title: 📏 Reading 'Whether It Be Good or Bad'
slides.subtitle: The same six words are made to support opposite conclusions

boxes.title: Rav for Reish Lakish
items: What has no distinction between good and bad? Temple maintenance — its sanctity is identical blemished or not
So the verse addresses maintenance consecrations
'And the priest shall value it' then excludes altar animals entirely

boxes.title: Rav for Rabbi Shimon
items: What does divide between good and bad? Altar consecrations
So the verse addresses altar animals
Difficulty: the verse would then have to read 'value it between good and bad' — the phrasing as written favors the Rabbis

boxes.title: What 'it' excludes for R' Yoḥanan
items: Not altar animals — those are included
Rather an animal blemished from the outset and consecrated for the altar
Difficulty: the school of Levi taught that everything is included, even such an animal, and even wild animals and geese

callout.label: The mechanism:
callout.text: The restrictive 'it' (אֹתָהּ) has to exclude something. Each amora spends it on a different case, and that choice is what their whole dispute reduces to.

slides.title: 📚 Two Baraitot on Consecrated Animals That Died
slides.subtitle: Each is a threatened refutation, and each is absorbed
rows: First: unblemished → buried, blemished → redeemed (altar); maintenance → always buried
R' Yoḥanan: it means blemished from the outset, which the Rabbis do exclude
Same baraita, read the other way
Reish Lakish: consecration preceded the blemish — and he reverses R' Shimon's clause in the text
Second: all buried (altar); maintenance redeemed if blemished
Seems to refute R' Yoḥanan again
R' Yoḥanan: again, blemished from the outset
R' Shimon does not dispute the altar case
Reish Lakish: he does dispute it — the text is to be understood accordingly

callout.label: The test used throughout:
callout.text: Whichever reading makes Rabbi Shimon's disagreement land in a sensible place is preferred — if a reading leaves him objecting to the wrong clause, or to none, it is rejected.

slides.title: 🐕 May One Redeem a Sacrificial Animal to Feed It to Dogs?
slides.subtitle: Rabbi Yirmeya presses Rabbi Zeira on a consequence of Reish Lakish

lines.speaker: R' Yirmeya
lines.text: On Reish Lakish's reading, an animal consecrated while unblemished, which then developed a blemish and died, is still redeemed. Shall we conclude that one may redeem sacrificial animals in order to feed them to dogs?

lines.speaker: Gemara
lines.text: No. When the baraita says the animals 'died', it does not mean natural death. The case is that he transgressed and slaughtered the blemished animals before redeeming them — and slaughter renders them fit for human consumption once redeemed.

lines.speaker: Baraita
lines.text: So it is taught: sacrificial animals that developed a blemish and were slaughtered — Rabbi Meir says they are buried, holding like Rabbi Shimon that altar animals are in standing and valuation.

lines.speaker: Baraita
lines.text: And the Rabbis say: since an altar animal is not in standing and valuation, even one already slaughtered may be redeemed.

lines.speaker: R' Yirmeya
lines.text: Then why does Rabbi Shimon bury unblemished maintenance animals, if he holds they were never in standing and valuation?

lines.speaker: R' Zeira
lines.text: Because they are fit for the altar. A baraita teaches that unblemished animals consecrated for maintenance are redeemed only for the altar — sold to someone obligated in an offering, never into non-sacred use.

callout.label: Why it matters:
callout.text: Redeeming an offering into dog food would degrade consecrated property; the Gemara avoids that conclusion by reading 'died' as 'was improperly slaughtered'.

slides.title: 🐐 An Animal Blemished Before It Was Ever Consecrated
slides.subtitle: Rav Pappa (or Rava) challenges Rabbi Yoḥanan from a mishna in Bekhorot

nodes.content: 📜 Bekhorot 14a: an animal whose permanent blemish preceded consecration is not sanctified as an offering — it is sold to buy a valid one
🐑 Consequences: firstborn status and priestly gifts apply, it may be shorn and worked, its offspring and milk are permitted, no karet outside, no temurah — and if it died, it is redeemed
❓ Rav Yehuda in Rav's name says this mishna follows Rabbi Shimon. But R' Yoḥanan said everyone agrees such an animal is excluded — so why single out R' Shimon?

columns.label: Abaye's first answer
columns.content: The 'Rabbis' who include even such an animal are a tanna of the school of Levi, not the Rabbis of the mishna

columns.label: Abaye's second answer
columns.content: Rav holds like Reish Lakish, so the mishna's latter clause cannot follow the Rabbis — or Rav does hold like R' Yoḥanan and did say 'R' Shimon and those who dispute him'

callout.label: R' Shimon's own concession:
callout.text: He agrees that an animal blemished from the outset and consecrated for the altar is redeemed if it died — 'the priest shall value it' excludes it.

slides.title: ⚱️ The New Mishna: Buried, or Burned?
slides.subtitle: Two lists of items from which benefit is forbidden

steps.content: 1️⃣ Buried: a sacrificial animal's miscarried fetus, and a miscarried placenta
2️⃣ Also buried: the stoned ox, the heifer whose neck is broken (egla arufa), the leper's birds, and the impure nazirite's shorn hair
3️⃣ Also buried: the firstborn donkey whose neck was broken, meat cooked in milk, and non-sacred animals slaughtered in the courtyard
4️⃣ Rabbi Shimon dissents: non-sacred animals slaughtered in the courtyard are burned, like disqualified offerings — and by rabbinic decree so is a wild animal slaughtered there
5️⃣ Burned: chametz on Pesach, impure teruma, orla and kilei hakerem — foods burned, liquids buried; and one may even light a fire with impure teruma bread and oil

callout.label: The organizing idea:
callout.text: Disposal follows the item's nature: what can be consumed by fire is burned, what cannot is buried — and the dispute over courtyard-slaughtered animals is about whether they are treated as sacred refuse or ordinary forbidden matter.

summary.principle: The restrictive word 'it' in 'the priest shall value it' must exclude something from standing and valuation — and the entire Yoḥanan–Reish Lakish dispute is a disagreement about which case it spends itself on.

flowSteps.content: 📏 'Whether good or bad' → Rav reads it for maintenance (Reish Lakish); the phrasing resists Rabbi Shimon's reading
📚 Two baraitot threaten each amora; each answers by fixing whether the blemish preceded or followed consecration

columns.content: 🐕 'Died' means improperly slaughtered — so no redeeming offerings into dog food
🐐 Blemished from the outset: R' Shimon concedes it is redeemed; the school of Levi includes even it

flowSteps.content: ⚱️ New mishna: miscarried fetus and placenta, stoned ox, egla arufa, leper's birds, nazirite's hair, meat in milk → buried
🎓 Key Principle: chametz, impure teruma, orla and kilei hakerem are burned when solid and buried when liquid — form of destruction follows form of the thing

quiz.q: How does Rav derive Reish Lakish's position from 'whether it be good or bad'?
o: Because blemished and unblemished altar animals have different sanctity
Because only Temple-maintenance consecrations have identical status whether blemished or not, so the verse must address them
Because the priest values only good animals
Because the verse mentions a non-kosher animal
quiz.e: Rav asks what item draws no distinction between good and bad, and answers: Temple maintenance. The restrictive 'it' then excludes altar animals from standing and valuation.

quiz.q: On Rabbi Yoḥanan's view, what does the restrictive word 'it' exclude?
o: Animals consecrated for the altar
Non-kosher animals
An animal blemished from the outset that was consecrated for the altar
Wild animals and birds
quiz.e: Since Rabbi Yoḥanan includes altar animals in standing and valuation, he must spend the exclusion elsewhere. This creates a difficulty from the school of Levi, which taught that even such an animal is included.

quiz.q: Why does the Gemara reject Rabbi Yirmeya's inference that one may redeem sacrificial animals to feed to dogs?
o: Because dogs may not eat consecrated meat under any circumstances
Because the baraita's 'died' means the animals were improperly slaughtered, which renders them fit for human consumption once redeemed
Because Reish Lakish retracted his position
Because blemished animals are never redeemed
quiz.e: Reading 'died' as natural death would force the degrading conclusion. The Gemara instead reads it as a transgressive slaughter before redemption, which leaves the meat fit for people.

quiz.q: Why, according to Rabbi Zeira, does Rabbi Shimon bury unblemished animals consecrated for Temple maintenance even though he holds they were never in standing and valuation?
o: Because they are fit for the altar, and such animals are redeemed only for the altar, never into non-sacred use
Because their sanctity is more severe than altar animals
Because the treasurer has no authority over them
Because they cannot be appraised by a priest
quiz.e: A baraita teaches that unblemished animals consecrated for maintenance are redeemed only by sale to someone obligated in an offering. Since no non-sacred redemption is available, a dead one is buried.

quiz.q: According to the new mishna, which of these is BURNED rather than buried?
o: A sacrificial animal's miscarried placenta
The hair of an impure nazirite
Impure teruma
A firstborn donkey whose neck was broken
quiz.e: Impure teruma appears on the burning list along with chametz, orla and kilei hakerem. The other three are on the burial list; Rabbi Shimon separately holds that non-sacred animals slaughtered in the courtyard are burned.
